newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Pro-Abacha parties take lead in Nigerian poll.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Abacha parties take lead in Nigerian poll.

text.p: Two political parties that want to adopt military ruler General Sani Abacha as their candidate for civilan-rule presidential elections took a lead in early official results of local polls released on Sunday.
Results of Saturday's voting from two of Nigeria's 36 states put the United Nigeria Congress Party (UNCP) and the Democratic Party of Nigeria (DPN) well ahead of three other parties.
Exit polls forecast a similar trend nationwide for the poll to elect chairmen and councillors for 774 municipalities.
The military government cited the peaceful local elections throughout the country as proof that its controversial civil rule plan was popular despite criticism in the West.
In Lagos state, which is centred around Nigeria's largest city and commercial capital, UNCP clinched eight council chairmanships from 13 declared, state radio announced.
DPN took three and a third party, Grassroots Democratic Movement (GDN), two. There will be a runoff in seven local authorities where no clear winner emerged, the radio said.
UNCP and DPN were neck and neck in northern Bauchi, winning six and five chairmanships respectively from 14 declared. One went to GDM while two go to a second round.
The independent Thisday and Concord dailies published separate exit polls conducted by their reporters nationwide predicting similar final results. They gave no precise figures.
"The indications do not depart significantly from the spread of the parties," Thisday said.
The trend appeared in line with the rating of the National Electoral Commission (NECON) when it registered five political parties last September after the army lifted a ban on parties.

NECON said UNCP had the widest nationwide support, followed by DPN. Both are centrist with their roots in the predominantly Islamic north, which has produced most of Nigeria's leaders since independence in 1960.
Many veteran politicians stayed on the sidelines because their parties were not registered by the military. They were expected to decide their affiliation after results are known.

The leadership of both the UNCP and the DPN have declared willingness to pick Abacha as their candidate for a presidential election due by September 1998 and leading to the military's promised handover of power the following month.

Abacha's only comment so far on the growing controversy about the prospect of his following other military leaders in West Africa by seeking to legitimise his rule through the ballot box is that it depends on his "constituency".
He has not explained if the constituency is the military or another group.
His supporters, however, say he is as free as anyone to contest elections once he quits the army.
Information Minister Walter Ofonagoro said the orderly and enthusiastic voting showed that Nigerians endorsed the government's programme to transfer power to civilians in 1998.
"That's the way elections should be," Ofonagoro told reporters after watching polling in the city of Kaduna. "We want to show the world that Nigeria is the father of democracy."
Local observers and Western diplomats who followed Saturday's polling said they were surprised by the relaxed manner of the voting.
More than 55 million people from a population of 100 million registered to vote.
Nigeria's then military rulers scrapped the 1993 poll as southern millionaire Moshood Abiola headed for victory and Abacha seized power in the confusion that followed.
